title: Hideo Nomo’s No-No Was the Toughest Ever
contentHtml:
Every no-hitter is special, to some degree or another. (Even though my feelings on the recent trend of combined no-nos are well-documented.) Setting down every opposing batter without allowing a hit is something to be celebrated — and even now, as we lament the decline of leaguewide batting averages, we haven’t seen a traditional single-pitcher no-hitter since Blake Snell on August 2, 2024, more than two full calendar years ago. This is not an easy thing to do to a major-league lineup under any circumstances.

Still, not all no-hitters are created equal. Some come against easier opponents, or under tougher hitting conditions at certain ballparks. When Juan Marichal no-hit the Houston Astros Colt .45s on Jun 15, 1963, for instance, it was one of those chilly (59° F) Candlestick Park days against a team that would lose 96 games in its second year of existence. It was a little bit easier to no-hit that squad than, say, Randy Johnson's perfecto versus the dynasty-era Atlanta Braves in 2004.

But the greatest, most unlikely no-no of all belongs to… Nomo.
